newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Shell sees pressure on refining margins in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Shell sees pressure on refining margins in 1997.

text.p: Shell Singapore said on Friday, short of major disruptions, there will be a continuing downward pressure on refinery margins in 1997 due to additional capacity which has come onstream in 1996.

"The underlying scenario, in our view is that, short of any major unforeseen disruptions, there will be continuing downward pressure on refinery margins in general, because of additional refining capacity which has come onstream in 1996," Shell said in a written response to a Reuter query.
"For example, during 1996/1997, South Korea will have added as much refinery capacity as is now present in Singapore and this is bound to affect export markets."
South Korea's refineries have added around 900,000 barrels barrels per day (bpd) of capacity in 1995/1996, compared with Singapore's total refining capacity of 1.23 million bpd.
But Shell said that overall they are "fully satisfied" with their performance over this year.

"On the whole, refinery margins have been a good deal better in 1996 than originally envisaged, helped by the very cold winter in the northern hemisphere in the early part of the year," a Shell spokeswoman said.
She said refining margins in the first quarter of next year are very much linked to global market conditions.
"If a cold winter prevails in the northern hemisphere, demand there for oil products will be strong and arbitrage cargoes looking for customers are likely to stay away from the Pacific," she said.
The spokeswoman said during 1996, Shell's scheduled shutdowns at its Bukom refinery, were both carried out according to plan.

According to earlier reports, the refinery's 200,000-bpd crude distiller-5 were shut for one-month maintenance in July. This unit was later operating at 70 percent capacity after it resumed operations in early August and then at 80 percent until early September because of poor refining margins.
Shell also shut its 35,000-bpd long residue catalytic cracker for more than five weeks, which resumed operations on Decemner 10.
The spokeswoman also said Asia Pacific is the fastest growing oil market in the world with demand growing at around four percent annually.
But it was unlikely that the market could absorb all of the new production immediately as refineries come in large "chunks", while demand tends to grow steadily, she said.
"Over time, we expect demand growth to absorb some of the new capacity," the spokeswoman said.

"We believe that there will continue to be growth opportunities for export refineries like Shell Singapore through our ability to meet changing quality needs and our flexibility and efficiency. But we can expect to face continuing competitive pressure from this increased capacity."
